cards.hook: We won’t move a loan just to move it.
cards.so_what: Already on a good rate? Ask what a switch adds, beyond the rate, before you break it.

posts.linkedin:
We won't move a loan just to move it.

Refinancing has real costs: break fees on a fixed rate, discharge and setup fees, and weeks of paperwork. If you're already on a good rate, especially a good fixed rate, a slightly sharper one rarely covers all of that.

So when someone asks us to refinance, the first question isn't "who's cheaper?" It's "what would the new loan do that this one can't?" A cash-out you genuinely need. A better split. An offset that actually gets used. If there's no real answer, we'd rather leave the loan where it is and tell you so.

Before you switch, ask what you're getting besides the rate.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.myth: Business cash should come from a business loan.
cards.reality: Credit against property is usually the cheapest business funding.
cards.because: Home-secured lending is priced well below overdrafts. It can go to the business under a loan agreement, with your accountant. Want the home kept out? We respect that.

posts.linkedin:
The cheapest business funding is often secured against your home, not the business.

When a business needs cash, most owners go straight to an overdraft or an unsecured business line of credit. Those are priced for the bank's risk, and it shows. Credit secured by residential property is usually priced well below them, and it can be lent on to the business under a proper loan agreement, set up with your accountant.

It is a trade-off, though: your home ends up backing the business. If you'd rather keep the family home out of it, we respect that, and we'll look at business-only options instead.

Either way, compare both before you sign up for the overdraft.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.hook: For a first home, we don’t think a buyer’s agent is worth the fee.
cards.so_what: You do the inspecting. We bring the sales data, due diligence and negotiation support.

posts.linkedin:
For a first home, we don't think a buyer's agent is worth the fee.

Buyer's agents typically charge around one to two percent of the price. On a high-ticket purchase that can earn its keep. For a first home bought in the general market, we'd rather you kept the money.

What matters most in a home you'll live in is how it feels when you walk through it, and only you can judge that. So you do the inspecting. We bring the property data, the due diligence, and help with pricing and negotiating the offer.

Before paying someone to search for you, ask what they'd know that you won't feel at the inspection.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.hook: Buying an investment with equity? How it’s set up matters for years.
cards.sub: Three setups we like, and why.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Keep the properties separate
cards.body: We fund the deposit and costs through a separate cash-out split against your home, without tying the two properties together. That keeps you flexible when you want to sell or refinance one later.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Park it in an offset
cards.body: Releasing equity before you’ve found the property? We often set it up interest-only with the funds sitting in an offset. Until you use it, your effective repayment is zero.

cards.label: investors
cards.title: Redraw isn’t a savings account
cards.body: Money in redraw has already paid down your home loan. Pulling it out to invest muddies what the loan is for. A separate split for investing is cleaner. Plan it with your accountant.

cards.label: investors
cards.headline: Get the structure right before you sign.
cards.body: A 15-minute chat is enough to map out the setup.

posts.linkedin:
Buying an investment with your home's equity? How it's set up matters for years.

Three setups we keep coming back to:

1. Keep the properties separate. Fund the deposit and costs through a separate split against your home, without tying the two properties together. You stay flexible when you sell or refinance one.

2. Park the equity in an offset. Released early and set up interest-only with the money sitting in an offset, it costs you nothing until you use it.

3. Don't treat redraw as savings. Pulling redraw out to invest muddies what the loan is for. A separate split is cleaner.

How the interest is treated for tax is one for your accountant.

General information only, not personal advice.
